Female Northern hogsuckers reach sexual maturity at a total length of 17 cm [Lp = 17 cm], a size typically attained after several growing seasons in the streams of the Mississippi River basin. At this length, the corresponding wet weight at puberty is approximately 38.2 grams [Wwp = approximately 38.2 grams], a body mass that reflects the energetic reserves required for vitellogenesis and the subsequent rigors of spawning migrations. Field studies using mark-recapture techniques have confirmed that individuals begin gonad maturation once they surpass this length threshold, with oocyte development proceeding through the late spring and early summer months. The timing of this transition appears closely tied to local thermal regimes and food availability, as females in more productive systems may reach the pubertal length earlier than those in oligotrophic headwater streams. Comparative data from related catostomids suggest that a 17 cm total length at puberty represents a moderate pace of maturation, neither as accelerated as some smaller-bodied suckers nor as delayed as the larger, longer-lived members of the genus Ictiobus. This life-history pattern places Hypentelium nigricans in an intermediate position among the Catostomidae, balancing early reproductive output against continued somatic growth.

The maximum reproductive rate of the Northern hogsucker has been quantified under controlled laboratory conditions at 13 °C [T = 13 °C], where females produce a single large clutch of eggs per spawning season [F_R_i = a single large clutch of eggs per spawning season]. Each clutch contains approximately 82 eggs [N_R_i = Each clutch contains approximately 82 eggs] on average following the application of a standardized hormonal induction protocol. This annual reproductive output, equivalent to roughly 82 eggs per year when extrapolated from the single seasonal spawning event, is modest compared to many freshwater cypriniforms of similar body size, which often display fractional spawning or multiple clutches over an extended breeding window. The relatively low fecundity is compensated by the large diameter of individual oocytes, which measure roughly 1.8 millimeters based on data from the congeneric Erimyzon oblongus. The resulting yolk reserves are substantial, providing newly hatched larvae with sufficient endogenous nutrition during the critical transition to exogenous feeding. At this stable temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C], embryonic development proceeds steadily, with chorion rupture occurring after approximately 10 to 14 days depending on dissolved oxygen levels.

The wet weight at birth for this species is estimated at 0.0031 grams [Wwb = 0.0031 grams], a value derived from the egg diameter of 1.8 millimeters observed in the closely related Eastern creek chubsucker, Erimyzon oblongus. Such a minute hatchling mass is typical of catostomid larvae, which emerge from the chorion as poorly developed, yolk-sac-dependent alevins. These prolarvae remain non-feeding for several days, relying exclusively on the endogenous yolk reserves absorbed from the large perivitelline space of the demersal egg. Field observations in Ozark streams indicate that newly hatched individuals drift downstream to slower, silt-laden pool habitats where they complete yolk-sac resorption. The transition to active feeding begins once the mouth opens and the yolk reserves are substantially depleted, a point that generally occurs at around 5 to 7 days post-hatch under the ambient stream temperatures typical of early summer. The 0.0031 gram mass at emergence is notably light when compared to the neonatal masses of other bottom-dwelling freshwater fishes, but it appears sufficient to sustain the larva through the brief period of yolk dependency before it begins capturing small zooplankton and chironomid larvae.

Under the stable thermal conditions that define the species' preferred habitat (13 °C [T = 13 °C]), the maximum recorded ultimate wet weight for an adult Northern hogsucker reaches 1980 grams [Wwi = 1980 grams]. This represents the heaviest individuals documented in long-term surveys of Missouri and Arkansas stream systems, where fish occasionally exceed 55 centimeters in total length. The ultimate total length corresponding to this peak body mass has been recorded at 61 cm [Li = 61 cm], a size that requires numerous growing seasons and consistently favorable conditions to attain. Such large specimens are exceptionally rare in modern collections, as most populations exhibit truncated size distributions due to angling pressure and habitat fragmentation. The asymptotic mass of 1980 grams is substantially greater than the pubertal mass of 38.2 grams, indicating a period of protracted somatic growth following the onset of sexual maturation. This growth trajectory is characteristic of an iteroparous, long-lived life history strategy, in which individuals continue to increase in body size and reproductive output well past the age of first reproduction. The largest individuals likely occupy high-quality riffle habitats with abundant cover and rich invertebrate prey bases.

Longevity records for captive-reared Northern hogsuckers maintained at 13 °C [T = 13 °C] indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 11 years [am = approximately 11 years], a duration that is considerable for a catostomid of this body size. Field-based mark-recapture studies have corroborated this estimate, with recaptured individuals bearing tags applied over a decade ago. This extended lifespan, combined with the delayed female maturation at 17 cm total length, underscores a relatively slow life-history pace that renders the species vulnerable to chronic anthropogenic stressors. Populations experiencing elevated water temperatures or reduced baseflow may experience shortened lifespans and diminished reproductive output. The total lifetime fecundity, while not directly measured, is likely to accumulate across repeated spawning seasons given the iteroparous strategy. The species' reliance on cool, well-oxygenated gravel riffles for spawning and larval development thus ties its demographic resilience directly to the preservation of thermal and hydrologic regimes characteristic of intact Eastern and Central U.S. stream ecosystems.
